## The write

`writeSearchSnapshot` and `writeProviderRecords` installed their artifact with
`os.MkdirAll` + `os.CreateTemp` + `os.Rename` on the joined path. `os.MkdirAll` follows a
symlinked directory component, so `<cache>/search` or `<cache>/search/search-snapshot-v12`
decided where the artifact actually landed.

`cacheEntry.writePath`'s comment argued that this was safe because "the cache directory is
caller-owned" and "anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache directory can write the
artifact directly". Both halves hold only while the cache directory is somewhere the caller
owns. `--cache-dir` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` take any path, including one inside the
scanned checkout, and then the planter is the repository — the same reasoning
`internal/cli/outputpath.go` already applies to `index --report` when the caller names a path
inside the checkout.

Reproduced against a scratch repository holding two committed `mode 120000` entries:

```
# .egcache/search -> /outside   (committed symlink, escapes the cache directory)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO/.egcache
  -> /outside/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz

# .git-linked family, cache directory at the checkout root
#   search -> .git   (committed symlink, stays inside the opened root)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO
  -> REPO/.git/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz
```

The destination filename is a digest, so this creates directories and files rather than
overwriting a chosen victim, and `os.Rename` already replaced a symlink at the artifact name
instead of following it. The directory components were the whole of the hole.

## The same defect is also a permanent cache miss

`cacheEntry.open` reads through `os.OpenRoot(cacheDir)`, which refuses exactly the components
the write followed — `TestCacheEntryReadRejectsSymlinkEscape` pins that. So a symlinked
descendant produced an entry that was **written on every run and read on none**. Measured on
the same repository and query, artifact mtime after two runs:

```
plain cache directory:      1787885558, 1787885558   (hit, not rewritten)
symlinked family component: 1787885508, 1787885561   (miss, rewritten every run)
```

That is why the refusal costs nothing that works today: every configuration it now rejects has
never produced a cache hit.

## The fix

`cacheEntry.write` replaces both bodies. The cache root stays caller-named and is still
resolved as given, so a symlinked cache *directory* — the deployment that puts the cache on
another volume, in a shared location, or outside a container's writable layer — keeps working
on both sides. Below the root, each component is created and then `Lstat`-checked before being
descended into through its own opened handle, and a symlink there is refused.

`os.Root` alone is not enough for the second half, for the reason `outputpath.go` records: it
stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays inside it, and with the cache
directory at a checkout root, `.git` is inside it. The `Lstat` check is not an exact-case
comparison, so a case-insensitive filesystem cannot answer it with a differently-spelled link.

The temporary file moves with it: a `crypto/rand` name opened `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` inside the
checked directory handle, keeping the `.snapshot-*.json.gz` / `.records-*.json.gz` shape that
cleanup globs match, and the install is `Rename` within that same handle.

Query-time caching is best effort and those call sites discard the error, so a refusal is a
cache miss there. `index`'s explicit persist reports it:

```
persist preindex snapshot: cache directory component "search" is a symlink
```

## Tests

`internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`, all five refusal assertions verified to fail
with the production change reverted and the tests kept:

- family component symlinked out of the cache directory (both families)
- family component symlinked to `.git`, staying inside the opened root (both families)
- version component symlinked out

plus three that pin what must not change: a symlinked cache root still round-trips at mode
0600, a symlink at the artifact name is replaced rather than written through, and a successful
write leaves only the artifact.

## Two existing tests changed, and why

`TestCacheWritesTolerateSymlinkedCacheDirectories` pinned the old behaviour, calling a symlinked
family subdirectory "a supported operator layout (a larger volume, a shared cache, an escape from
a container's writable layer)" whose artifact "must still be written **and read back through it**".

The read-back half was never true, and nothing asserted it. Every one of those three motivations
needs a link that LEAVES the cache directory, and that is exactly what the reader refuses.
Measured on unmodified `main`, with `cache/search -> ../backing`:

```
write:     ok, artifact lands in backing/v1/<key>.json.gz
read back: openat search/v1/<key>.json.gz: path escapes from parent
```

The only family link that does round-trip is one pointing back inside the cache directory, which
cannot reach another volume. So the test is replaced by
`TestCacheWritesRefuseSymlinkedFamilyDirectories`, which pins both halves: an artifact placed
behind the link by hand is still unreachable through it, and the write no longer pretends
otherwise.

`TestSearchCacheLoadersRejectSymlinkEscape`'s last block asserted that `preindex` persists beneath
such a cache directory. It now asserts the refusal and that the message names the component: an
entry the durability read cannot see is not a durable artifact, so reporting it is the honest
outcome for a verb whose whole job is to promise one.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l` clean, and `go test ./...` green across every package
(`internal/sem` 863s, `internal/cli` 153s under load).

CI is green on all three platforms, including the Windows mode-bits fix in the second commit.

`TestWriteOutputFileDoesNotFollowALinkSwappedInAfterTheCheck`

unmodified `origin/main` worktree, which is why it was reported as unrelated to this change. CI has
since run it on all three platforms and it passes, so it was local starvation (the test spins until
it wins a race, and this machine was running several suites concurrently), not a non-termination.
Nothing is outstanding against it.

Every claim above was reproduced by driving the built binary against a scratch repository with
committed `mode 120000` entries, before and after, for both cache families.

The guard tested `info.Mode()&fs.ModeSymlink != 0`. A junction planted at the `family` or `version` component therefore passed the check and was then descended into and followed — exactly the redirect this guard exists to refuse.

This repository already had the correct predicate, with five production call sites:

```
internal/sem/path_redirect_windows.go:12   return info.Mode()&(os.ModeSymlink|os.ModeIrregular) != 0
internal/sem/path_redirect_other.go:8      return info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0
```

---

### 2. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:194` — `rand.Text()` terminates the process — **VALID** (and stronger than described)

Verified in the toolchain's own source. `crypto/rand.Text` calls `Read`, and `crypto/rand/rand.go`:

```go
// Read calls [io.ReadFull] on [Reader] and crashes the program irrecoverably if
// an error is returned. …
	if err != nil {
		fatal("crypto/rand: failed to read random data (see https://go.dev/issue/66821): " + err.Error())
		panic("unreachable") // To be sure.
	}
```

`fatal` is `runtime.fatal` via `go:linkname`, reaching `fatalthrow` — the runtime's unrecoverable throw. So it is **not** a panic a caller can `recover`; it is a hard process kill. Tearing down a whole index run because a temporary cache file could not be named is the wrong failure mode for a best-effort write whose errors every caller already discards.

For contrast, `os.CreateTemp` never has this exposure: `$GOROOT/src/os/tempfile.go` names its files from `runtime.rand()`, an infallible non-cryptographic source. **Fix:** `cacheTempNameSuffix(source io.Reader)` reads 16 bytes with `io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, …)` and hex-encodes them — same CSPRNG, error returned instead of a process kill.

Standalone probe against the same toolchain (`go1.26.0 darwin/arm64`), exercising every operation this code performs through the returned handle:

```
B OpenRoot(link -> ABS outside path):    ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
C OpenRoot(link -> sibling INSIDE root): OK (no error)
C sub.Open(in.txt):                      SUCCESS, read "INSIDE-BYTES"
D OpenFile(link/x -> ../outside REL):    ERROR: openat link/x: path escapes from parent
E OpenFile(link/y -> ABS outside path):  ERROR: openat link/y: path escapes from parent
F Rename(src.txt -> link/z.txt):         ERROR: renameat src.txt link/z.txt: path escapes from parent
```

`go doc os.Root`:

> Methods on Root will follow symbolic links, but symbolic links may not reference a location outside the root. Symbolic links must not be absolute.

No change made. Closing the window would mean re-deriving through a handle `os.Root` already re-derives, for an outcome `os.Root` already guarantees.

## Impact

`graph doctor --json` is the pre-flight entire-brain runs before every snapshot (`internal/cli/semantic.go:946` on the consumer side). It reports the repo root, provider name, version and no-egress posture — but not the two values a consumer actually needs to know the snapshot will be usable:

- the `repo_key` this binary will stamp into the header, and
- the `schema_version` it speaks.

Both are discoverable only from the finished snapshot. So a repo_key rule mismatch or an unsupported schema major costs a whole snapshot run — up to the consumer's 30-minute deadline on a large repository — before it surfaces. And with nothing advertised, the consumer is left reimplementing the repo_key rule in order to predict what it should have received; that is exactly how the two sides drifted apart (see entire-brain `audit/seam-repo-key`, where four of five remote shapes failed because the consumer's guess and this binary's rule disagreed).

The repo_key rule is not an internal detail. It is the symbol-ID namespace, it is deliberately derived from the repository alone so another process *can* reproduce it, and a consumer must be able to predict it to tell a snapshot of the requested repository apart from a foreign one.

## Fix

- `sem.RepoKey` exports the rule with the contract stated on it.
- `doctor --json` reports `repo_key` and `schema_version` beside `repo_root`. Purely additive, so an older consumer that ignores unknown fields is unaffected (ADR 0001 rule 3).

## Verification

- `TestDoctorReportsRepoKeyAndSchemaVersion` — github, no-remote and gitlab repositories.
- `TestDoctorRepoKeyMatchesSnapshotHeader` — the anti-drift gate: what doctor advertises must be byte-identical to what the provider itself computes, or the handshake is worse than no handshake.
- `TestRepoKeyContractGoldenVectors` — pins the rule's vectors; entire-brain asserts the same table on its side.
- Mutation-verified: making doctor compute the key by a different rule than the provider fails the tests.
- Full suite green.

## Impact

`graph doctor --json` is the pre-flight entire-brain runs before every snapshot (`internal/cli/semantic.go:946` on the consumer side). It reports the repo root, provider name, version and no-egress posture — but not the two values a consumer actually needs to know the snapshot will be usable:


Note the failing shapes are broader than the report: `gh/org-a/tools` vs `gh/org-b/tools`
is fine — the github half of the rule is unique. It is everything *else* that collapses:
no remote, gitlab, bitbucket, self-hosted. `local/<basename>` is a directory name.

### It does not corrupt or leak anything today

Four experiments, one shared cache dir throughout.

**1. No shared entry, no eviction, no overwrite.** Indexing A then B writes two entries:

```
$ entire-graph index --repo .../x/tools --cache-dir $C   # entries: 1
$ entire-graph index --repo .../y/tools --cache-dir $C   # entries: 2
CACHE/search/search-snapshot-v12/fd37fa51...json.gz
CACHE/search/search-snapshot-v12/2c7efeb8...json.gz
```

Same for the other cache family via `snapshot`: `CACHE/records/provider-records-v8/{5252094d,257da052}...`.
Those are the only two families (`newCacheEntry` call sites: `search_cache.go:136,201,246,381`,
`records_cache.go:136`).

**2. Not even at an identical tree.** The adversarial case — same key, same tree hash, so
every other keyed term agrees:

```
trees: beef6992301dd4f9f921beff64aca6dc8dcd29ff vs beef6992301dd4f9f921beff64aca6dc8dcd29ff
cache entries after p=1 after q=2   (identical tree, identical repo_key, different path)
```

Because both key functions hash the absolute repository path beside the repo key —
`searchSnapshotKey` `internal/sem/search_cache.go:752`, `providerRecordsKey`
`internal/sem/records_cache.go:62`.

**3. No cross-repo leakage.** Each repository's only symbol is invisible to the other:

```
$ entire-graph search --repo .../x/tools --head --cache-dir $C --query BetaOnlySecretWidget
results: ['local/tools:Go:alpha.go:function:AlphaOnlySecretWidget']
$ entire-graph search --repo .../y/tools --head --cache-dir $C --query AlphaOnlySecretWidget
results: ['local/tools:Go:beta.go:function:BetaOnlySecretWidget']
```

**4. The key never reaches a filesystem path.** Cache paths are `family/version/<sha256hex>.json.gz`
and `newCacheEntry` rejects anything else (`cache_entry.go:30`, `validSHA256Hex`). The `/` in
`local/tools` is inert; there is no path-safety exposure to fix.

### The existing repo-key-mismatch machinery MISSES this case — and it does not matter

`validCachedSearchSnapshot` (`search_cache.go:807`), `selectiveSearchSnapshotFromFull`
(`:535`), and the records `Store` provenance check (`records_cache.go:181`) all compare
`RepoKey` for equality. Two colliding keys compare equal, so every one of them passes. They
never get the chance to matter, because the `repository-path` term in the cache key means a
colliding entry is never looked up in the first place. They are defence in depth; the path
is the discriminator. ADR 0002 already says as much — it kept the checkout path in the key
and listed identity-only keying as a change it explicitly did not take.

### The consumer is not affected either

`entire-brain` never uses this string as a storage key. Its own key
(`internal/cli/env.go:344-353`) is `local/<base>-<sha256(abs path)[:12]>`, and every durable
store hangs off it — facts dir, semantic snapshots, pattern sqlite, `gitmeta.git`, workspace
members. Its own commit states the invariant: *"the hash suffix is load-bearing: two
checkouts sharing a basename must not collide onto one brain."* Its on-disk gate compares
against that path-hashed key, so a colliding provider key can never pass it — the shipped
check is over-strict, not under-strict, which is the *other* seam bug this PR exists to fix.
The only place a `local/<basename>` gate is admitted is unmerged brain work, and there the
bundle manifest still carries the path-hashed key and rejects first.

### Decision: fix the contract, not the key

Re-keying `local/*` — a path hash, or extending the remote rule to every host — would:

- rewrite **every symbol ID in every non-github repository** (`repoKey:language:path:kind:name`),
  orphaning anything downstream keyed by ID;
- break `TestRepoKeyContractGoldenVectors`, which is asserted on *both* sides of the seam,
  while brain has in-flight branches built against the current vectors;
- for a path hash, make the key **machine-local**, so a gitlab or self-hosted repository's
  symbol IDs would stop being portable between a laptop and CI.

That is a real regression traded for a collision that no measurement here shows corrupting
anything. So the key is unchanged, and the sentence that was wrong is now right.

`e3850959`:

- `internal/sem/provider.go` — `RepoKey` states the boundary: it is a **namespace, not a
  repository identity**; only the `gh/` half is globally unique; `repo_key` mismatch proves
  a foreign snapshot, `repo_key` match does not prove a native one; `repo_root` (already in
  the same doctor report) is the discriminator, which is exactly what this provider's cache
  keys and brain's storage key both already do.
- `docs/snapshot-format.md` — the same boundary where a consumer reads the header format.
- `TestRepoKeyLocalIsNotGloballyUnique` — pins the collision, and pins that two github owners
  do *not* collide. The doc cannot quietly start claiming uniqueness again.
- `TestCollidingRepoKeysDoNotShareCacheEntries` — the guard that keeps the collision inert:
  same key, identical tree, one cache dir, two entries, each reporting its own `repo_root`.

That second test is not decorative. Dropping the path term — the change ADR 0002 names as
possible future work — produces this today:

```
MUTANT: index p  ->  repo_root=.../same/p/tools  hit=False
MUTANT: index q  ->  repo_root=.../same/p/tools  hit=True     <== q reports P's root
MUTANT: search q ->  repo_root=.../same/p/tools
entries: 1
```

A foreign snapshot handed to a consumer under a matching `repo_key`. The test stops that
landing while `local/<basename>` can collide.

### Verification

Mutation-verified in both directions, each grep-confirmed applied and compiling:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop `repository-path` from `searchSnapshotKey` | `TestCollidingRepoKeysDoNotShareCacheEntries` FAILS — *"reported a cache hit; a colliding repository's entry was served"* |
| give `repoKey` a path-hash suffix | `TestRepoKeyLocalIsNotGloballyUnique` FAILS — *"local repo keys = "local/tools-MUT2aecae269" and "local/tools-MUT217578f9a""* |
| restore both | all pass |

`go test ./internal/cli` green (22.8s), `go test ./internal/sem -run 'RepoKey|SearchSnapshotKey|CacheKey'` green,
`gofmt`/`go vet` clean.

### Left open

- The provider still cannot reproduce brain's storage key, and brain's shipped on-disk gate

  its unmerged `audit/job1-repokey` addresses; this PR's `doctor` handshake is the input it

- A repository directory name containing `:` produces an ambiguous-looking stable ID

  strings, never split — but a consumer that parses one by `:` would mis-split it. Separate
  issue, not touched.

### Repro

`resolveRepo` returns its input verbatim and falls back to `"."`:

```
internal/cli/root.go:920   if env.RepoRoot != "" { return env.RepoRoot, nil }
```

Every path that actually **builds** a snapshot derives the key from the absolutised path:

```

internal/sem/provider.go:1455   key = repoKey(ctx, absRepo)
internal/sem/search_cache.go:126, 196, 343   repoKey(ctx, absRepo)
internal/sem/records_cache.go:123            repoKey(ctx, absRepo)
```

`doctor` was the only caller passing an unnormalised path. Since the `local/` half of the rule is `"local/" + filepath.Base(repo)`, the two disagreed for any unnormalised spelling. Reproduced on the branch before the fix — this is the literal `doctor --json` output:

```json
{"repo_key":"local/..","repo_root":"…/001/sub/..", …}
```

`local/.` is a namespace shared by **every** repository on the machine, and it is never the namespace the snapshot itself carries. Every in-process caller already passes the absolute path the provider derived, so it is a no-op for them; the exported `RepoKey` has no such guarantee — `doctor` resolves the repository from `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`, `--repo` or the working directory, any of which may arrive relative or uncleaned. `report["repo_root"]` is deliberately left reporting what the caller asked for; only the key is normalised.

the file path is escaped, so a directory named `weird:name` — or an ordinary

whose kind field cannot contain a ':'. Nothing pinned that, so a future

repository silently.

## Impact

`graph doctor --json` is the pre-flight entire-brain runs before every snapshot (`internal/cli/semantic.go:946` on the consumer side). It reports the repo root, provider name, version and no-egress posture — but not the two values a consumer actually needs to know the snapshot will be usable:

- the `repo_key` this binary will stamp into the header, and
- the `schema_version` it speaks.

Both are discoverable only from the finished snapshot. So a repo_key rule mismatch or an unsupported schema major costs a whole snapshot run — up to the consumer's 30-minute deadline on a large repository — before it surfaces. And with nothing advertised, the consumer is left reimplementing the repo_key rule in order to predict what it should have received; that is exactly how the two sides drifted apart (see entire-brain `audit/seam-repo-key`, where four of five remote shapes failed because the consumer's guess and this binary's rule disagreed).

The repo_key rule is not an internal detail. It is the symbol-ID namespace, it is deliberately derived from the repository alone so another process *can* reproduce it, and a consumer must be able to predict it to tell a snapshot of the requested repository apart from a foreign one.

## Fix

- `sem.RepoKey` exports the rule with the contract stated on it.
- `doctor --json` reports `repo_key` and `schema_version` beside `repo_root`. Purely additive, so an older consumer that ignores unknown fields is unaffected (ADR 0001 rule 3).

## Verification

- `TestDoctorReportsRepoKeyAndSchemaVersion` — github, no-remote and gitlab repositories.
- `TestDoctorRepoKeyMatchesSnapshotHeader` — the anti-drift gate: what doctor advertises must be byte-identical to what the provider itself computes, or the handshake is worse than no handshake.
- `TestRepoKeyContractGoldenVectors` — pins the rule's vectors; entire-brain asserts the same table on its side.
- Mutation-verified: making doctor compute the key by a different rule than the provider fails the tests.
- Full suite green.

Two unrelated repositories, different content, different symbols, same basename:

```

local/tools
$ (cd /tmp/.../collide/y/tools && entire-graph doctor --json) | jq -r .repo_key
```

```
$ entire-graph index --repo .../y/tools --cache-dir $C   # entries: 2
```

**VALID.** Head is now `8bf16e8d`.

### What was wrong

`resolveRepo` returns its input verbatim and falls back to `"."`:

```
internal/cli/root.go:917   if explicit != "" { return explicit, nil }
internal/cli/root.go:920   if env.RepoRoot != "" { return env.RepoRoot, nil }
internal/cli/root.go:940   return ".", nil
```

Every path that actually **builds** a snapshot derives the key from the absolutised path:

```
internal/sem/provider.go:1445   absRepo, err := filepath.Abs(repo)
internal/sem/provider.go:1455   key = repoKey(ctx, absRepo)
internal/sem/search_cache.go:126, 196, 343   repoKey(ctx, absRepo)
internal/sem/records_cache.go:123            repoKey(ctx, absRepo)
```

`doctor` was the only caller passing an unnormalised path. Since the `local/` half of the rule is `"local/" + filepath.Base(repo)`, the two disagreed for any unnormalised spelling. Reproduced on the branch before the fix — this is the literal `doctor --json` output:

```json
{"repo_key":"local/.","repo_root":".", …}
{"repo_key":"local/..","repo_root":"…/001/sub/..", …}
{"repo_key":"local/.","repo_root":"…/001/.", …}
```

`local/.` is a namespace shared by **every** repository on the machine, and it is never the namespace the snapshot itself carries. That inverts the point of publishing the key before a run: a consumer comparing its own prediction against `local/.` rejects a native snapshot, or accepts a foreign one, on a value nothing produces. `TestDoctorRepoKeyMatchesSnapshotHeader` calls itself the anti-drift gate, but it only ever passed an absolute path, so it never exercised this.

### Fix

`internal/sem/provider.go` — `repoKey` normalises the caller's spelling first:

```go
repo = absoluteRepoPath(repo)   // filepath.Abs, with the original kept as fallback
```

Placed at the rule rather than at the one call site. Every in-process caller already passes the absolute path the provider derived, so it is a no-op for them; the exported `RepoKey` has no such guarantee — `doctor` resolves the repository from `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`, `--repo` or the working directory, any of which may arrive relative or uncleaned. Normalising here is what keeps the documented promise that the key is reproducible from a path alone.

`report["repo_root"]` is deliberately left reporting what the caller asked for; only the key is normalised.

### Test

`TestDoctorRepoKeyIsIndependentOfHowTheRepoRootIsSpelled` in `internal/cli/doctor_repo_key_test.go`, running `doctor --json` end to end over four spellings of the same repository — absolute, `"."` (with `t.Chdir`), `<repo>/sub/..`, and `<repo>/.` — all of which must report `local/<basename>`.

### Mutation verification

Removed the `repo = absoluteRepoPath(repo)` line, `grep`-confirmed only the helper's definition and doc comment remained with no call site, rebuilt (the unused function still compiles):

```
--- FAIL: …/working_directory
    doctor repo_key for root "." = local/., want "local/001"
--- FAIL: …/uncleaned_absolute
    doctor repo_key for root "…/001/sub/.." = local/.., want "local/001"
--- FAIL: …/trailing_dot
    doctor repo_key for root "…/001/." = local/., want "local/001"
```

Restored, `grep`-confirmed the call back, all four subtests pass. Full `go test ./internal/cli` passes (25s), and `go test ./internal/sem -run 'RepoKey|Cache'` passes — the cache keys fold `repoKey` in, and they were already passing absolute paths, so nothing there moves. `go vet` and `gofmt -l` clean.

`graph doctor --json` is the pre-flight entire-brain runs before every snapshot.
It reports the repo root, the provider name, the version, and the no-egress
posture — but not the two values the consumer actually needs in order to know
the snapshot will be usable: the `repo_key` this binary will stamp into the
header, and the `schema_version` it speaks.

Both are discoverable only from the finished snapshot today. A repo_key rule
mismatch or an unsupported schema major therefore costs an entire snapshot run
(up to 30 minutes on a large repository) before it surfaces, and the consumer is
left reimplementing the repo_key rule to predict what it should have received.

The repo_key rule is not an internal detail: it is the symbol-ID namespace, it
is derived from the repository alone precisely so another process can reproduce
it, and entire-brain must be able to predict it to tell a snapshot of the
requested repository apart from a foreign one.

- `sem.RepoKey` exports the rule with the contract stated on it.
- `doctor --json` reports `repo_key` and `schema_version` beside `repo_root`.
- `TestDoctorRepoKeyMatchesSnapshotHeader` is the anti-drift gate: what doctor
  advertises must be byte-identical to what the snapshot header carries, or the
  handshake is worse than no handshake.
- `TestRepoKeyContractGoldenVectors` pins the rule's vectors. entire-brain
  asserts the same table on its side, so changing the rule in either repository
  breaks a test in both instead of silently splitting the seam.","messageHeadline":"fix(doctor): the provider never tells a consumer which repo_key or sc…","oid":"1491e49f94496a5279c2591fcacf298f09a7f1e2"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-29T21:41:29Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-29T21:41:29Z","messageBody":"…lf is unique

The handshake this PR publishes stated that a consumer can predict repo_key
"to tell a snapshot of THIS repository apart from a foreign one". Measured,
that is false for half the rule: `local/<basename>` is the directory name, so
/x/tools and /y/tools — two unrelated repositories, different content,
different symbols — both advertise `local/tools` from `doctor --json` and both
stamp `local/tools` into every symbol ID. A consumer comparing the advertised
key against a received header accepts the foreign snapshot.

Measured what the collision actually costs, before changing anything:

  - Nothing in this provider. Both persistent cache families hash the absolute
    repository path beside the repo key (searchSnapshotKey:752,
    providerRecordsKey:62), so two colliding repositories sharing one cache dir
    get two entries and two graphs — even at a byte-identical tree, where every
    other keyed term agrees. No eviction, no overwrite, no cross-repo hit.
  - No leakage. Searching either repository for the other's only symbol returns
    only its own.
  - The existing repo-key equality gates (validCachedSearchSnapshot,
    selectiveSearchSnapshotFromFull, records Store) do MISS the collision — two
    colliding keys compare equal — but the path term means they never get the
    chance to matter. They are defence in depth, not the discriminator.

So the key is not changed. Re-keying `local/*` would rewrite every symbol ID in
every non-github repository, break the golden-vector table asserted on both
sides of the seam, and make the key machine-local — trading portability for a
collision that no measurement shows corrupting anything.

What changes is the contract, which is now honest about its own boundary:
repo_key is a necessary and not a sufficient identity test, and repo_root —
already reported beside it — is the discriminator. Two tests pin it:

  - TestRepoKeyLocalIsNotGloballyUnique — two same-named repositories collide,
    two github owners do not. The doc cannot quietly start claiming uniqueness.
  - TestCollidingRepoKeysDoNotShareCacheEntries — the guard that keeps the
    collision inert. ADR 0002 names identity-only cache keying as a future
    change it deliberately did not take; dropping the path term today serves
    the second repository the first's entry and reports the FIRST repository's
    root as its own, which is exactly a foreign snapshot under a matching key.

Mutation-verified both ways: removing the path term from searchSnapshotKey
fails the cache guard, and giving repoKey a path-hash suffix fails the
uniqueness pin.","messageHeadline":"docs(sem): repo_key is a namespace, not an identity — only its gh/ ha…","oid":"e38509597eb41bc495e194c5f6506c659e332481"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-29T22:08:43Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-29T22:08:43Z","messageBody":"…ymbol-ID parser

A local repo key is `local/<basename>`, and a symbol ID is
`repoKey:language:path:kind:qualifiedName` joined with ':'. Neither the key nor
the file path is escaped, so a directory named `weird:name` — or an ordinary
directory holding `od:d/mod.py` — emits IDs with more ':'-separated fields than
the format names, shifting every field for anyone who splits an ID positionally.

That is harmless only because no parser here does. Each one compares the whole
ID, anchors on the LAST separator, or is gated to the `external:` namespace
whose kind field cannot contain a ':'. Nothing pinned that, so a future
`strings.Split(id, ":")[2]` would have mis-attributed every symbol in such a
repository silently.

Covers goMethodSymbolByID, enclosingTypeShortName, externalParts, idMatches,
defExternalTypeName and parseSymbolRef at the unit level, plus symbols, edges,
neighbors and def end-to-end against a ':'-named repository. Each of the six
parsers was rewritten into its naive positional form to confirm the tests fail.

Unix-only: ':' is not a legal path character on Windows.","messageHeadline":"test(sem): pin that a ':' in a repo key or file path survives every s…","oid":"8baeea15096055841e3d95f125b7f4de19135617"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-29T22:08:53Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-29T22:08:53Z","messageBody":"…it positionally

The format was documented as `<repo-key>:<language>:<file-path>:<kind>:<qualified-name>`
with nothing said about escaping, which reads as an invitation to parse an ID by
splitting on ':' and indexing. Two of those fields can carry a ':' of their own:
a `local/<basename>` key inherits whatever the directory is called, and a file
path may contain one on any POSIX filesystem. A consumer reading
`split(id, ":")[2]` as the path mis-attributes every record in such a
repository, silently and without an error — a downstream consumer had already
encoded the opposite premise in a comment.

States the hazard next to the existing repo_key paragraph in the consumer
contract, and names the four safe reads: compare a whole ID, anchor on the LAST
separator for a trailing segment, cut at the FIRST separator only inside
`external:<kind>:<value>`, and take a path from the record's own `file_path`.","messageHeadline":"docs(sem): symbol ID fields are unescaped, so an ID must never be spl…","oid":"9da979f78706b328571605ac24607adb3885e223"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-30T15:23:12Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-30T15:23:12Z","messageBody":"The handshake published a key no build would emit. resolveRepo returns

Each fails on unpatched `main` and passes here. ## 1. `is_reference` on type relationships `is_reference` does not mean "this is a reference". It tells a consumer to **merge the related symbol's references into this one's**. Setting it on every `IMPLEMENTS`/`EXTENDS`/`INHERITS` made Find References on a base type report every subtype's *definition* as a reference to it. ## The write

`writeSearchSnapshot` and `writeProviderRecords` installed their artifact with
`os.MkdirAll` + `os.CreateTemp` + `os.Rename` on the joined path. `os.MkdirAll` follows a
symlinked directory component, so `<cache>/search` or `<cache>/search/search-snapshot-v12`
decided where the artifact actually landed.

`cacheEntry.writePath`'s comment argued that this was safe because "the cache directory is
caller-owned" and "anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache directory can write the
artifact directly". Both halves hold only while the cache directory is somewhere the caller
owns. `--cache-dir` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` take any path, including one inside the
scanned checkout, and then the planter is the repository — the same reasoning
`internal/cli/outputpath.go` already applies to `index --report` when the caller names a path
inside the checkout.

Reproduced against a scratch repository holding two committed `mode 120000` entries:

```
# .egcache/search -> /outside   (committed symlink, escapes the cache directory)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO/.egcache
  -> /outside/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz

# .git-linked family, cache directory at the checkout root
#   search -> .git   (committed symlink, stays inside the opened root)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO
  -> REPO/.git/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz
```

The destination filename is a digest, so this creates directories and files rather than
overwriting a chosen victim, and `os.Rename` already replaced a symlink at the artifact name
instead of following it. The directory components were the whole of the hole.

## The same defect is also a permanent cache miss

`cacheEntry.open` reads through `os.OpenRoot(cacheDir)`, which refuses exactly the components
the write followed — `TestCacheEntryReadRejectsSymlinkEscape` pins that. So a symlinked
descendant produced an entry that was **written on every run and read on none**. Measured on
the same repository and query, artifact mtime after two runs:

```
plain cache directory:      1787885558, 1787885558   (hit, not rewritten)
symlinked family component: 1787885508, 1787885561   (miss, rewritten every run)
```

That is why the refusal costs nothing that works today: every configuration it now rejects has
never produced a cache hit.

## The fix

`cacheEntry.write` replaces both bodies. The cache root stays caller-named and is still
resolved as given, so a symlinked cache *directory* — the deployment that puts the cache on
another volume, in a shared location, or outside a container's writable layer — keeps working
on both sides. Below the root, each component is created and then `Lstat`-checked before being
descended into through its own opened handle, and a symlink there is refused.

`os.Root` alone is not enough for the second half, for the reason `outputpath.go` records: it
stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays inside it, and with the cache
directory at a checkout root, `.git` is inside it. The `Lstat` check is not an exact-case
comparison, so a case-insensitive filesystem cannot answer it with a differently-spelled link.

The temporary file moves with it: a `crypto/rand` name opened `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` inside the
checked directory handle, keeping the `.snapshot-*.json.gz` / `.records-*.json.gz` shape that
cleanup globs match, and the install is `Rename` within that same handle.

Query-time caching is best effort and those call sites discard the error, so a refusal is a
cache miss there. `index`'s explicit persist reports it:

```
persist preindex snapshot: cache directory component "search" is a symlink
```

## Tests

`internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`, all five refusal assertions verified to fail
with the production change reverted and the tests kept:

- family component symlinked out of the cache directory (both families)
- family component symlinked to `.git`, staying inside the opened root (both families)
- version component symlinked out

plus three that pin what must not change: a symlinked cache root still round-trips at mode
0600, a symlink at the artifact name is replaced rather than written through, and a successful
write leaves only the artifact.

## Two existing tests changed, and why

`TestCacheWritesTolerateSymlinkedCacheDirectories` pinned the old behaviour, calling a symlinked
family subdirectory "a supported operator layout (a larger volume, a shared cache, an escape from
a container's writable layer)" whose artifact "must still be written **and read back through it**".

The read-back half was never true, and nothing asserted it. Every one of those three motivations
needs a link that LEAVES the cache directory, and that is exactly what the reader refuses.
Measured on unmodified `main`, with `cache/search -> ../backing`:

```
write:     ok, artifact lands in backing/v1/<key>.json.gz
read back: openat search/v1/<key>.json.gz: path escapes from parent
```

The only family link that does round-trip is one pointing back inside the cache directory, which
cannot reach another volume. So the test is replaced by
`TestCacheWritesRefuseSymlinkedFamilyDirectories`, which pins both halves: an artifact placed
behind the link by hand is still unreachable through it, and the write no longer pretends
otherwise.

`TestSearchCacheLoadersRejectSymlinkEscape`'s last block asserted that `preindex` persists beneath
such a cache directory. It now asserts the refusal and that the message names the component: an
entry the durability read cannot see is not a durable artifact, so reporting it is the honest
outcome for a verb whose whole job is to promise one.

Three of the findings the trail's review raised against #97, after it merged. Each fails on
unpatched `main` and passes here.

## 1. `is_reference` on type relationships

`is_reference` does not mean "this is a reference". It tells a consumer to **merge the related
symbol's references into this one's**. Setting it on every `IMPLEMENTS`/`EXTENDS`/`INHERITS` made
Find References on a base type report every subtype's *definition* as a reference to it.

Now set only for member-level relationships — a method override, where reaching the override's
callers from the base is the whole point. `is_implementation` continues to be set for the family.

## 2. Unrepresented containment

`DEFINES` and `CONTAINS` are skipped as redundant, because symbol metadata already carries the
membership via `EnclosingSymbol`. That holds **only when the relation agrees with `ContainerID`**.

An extension member — a method attached to a receiver declared elsewhere — produces a `CONTAINS`
whose parent is *not* the symbol's container. That membership exists in no other field, so skipping
it silently let the note report a completeness the protobuf did not have. Two such relations exist
in this repository.

### The over-count this nearly shipped

My first version of that check also fired for `DEFINES` — a file defines a symbol whose
`ContainerID` is not the file — and reported **all 9,877** `DEFINES` relations as lost. `DEFINES` is
always represented, by the definition occurrence and the symbol record.

Caught by running a real export and reading the note, not by the unit tests, which all passed. A
test now pins `DEFINES` at zero, because the failure mode was a note that **overstated** loss — the
harder direction to notice, since nothing downstream complains about a projection claiming to have
dropped more than it did.

## 3. Cargo workspace inheritance

Only a literal `version` in `[package]` was read, so a crate using `version.workspace = true` or
`version = { workspace = true }` with the version in `[workspace.package]` exported as `0` —
collapsing distinct releases into one SCIP package identity, which is the exact confusion the
version field was changed to prevent.

Both spellings now resolve to `[workspace.package]`. A literal version still wins, and declaring
inheritance without a workspace version yields no version rather than a guess.

## Deliberately not included

**The reference-position problem** from the same review. That is a larger question about what the
export may legitimately claim, proposed separately in **RFD 0006 (#152)** rather than decided in a
follow-up PR. It would change reference occurrences from 25,716 to ~48 here, which is a decision,
not a fix.

**The two moniker findings** — external symbols minted in this repository's package rather than the
defining dependency's, and descriptors omitting container ancestry. Both rewrite every symbol's
identity, so they belong together with the moniker decision in RFD 0005's open question 2 rather
than being patched piecemeal.

## Gate

`gofmt -s -l .` empty · `go vet ./...` clean · `go build ./...` clean · `go test ./...` green across
all 8 packages.

Red on unpatched `main`:

```

--- FAIL: TestSCIPIsReferenceOnlyForMemberRelationships/type_implements

--- FAIL: TestScipProjectVersionReadsRootManifests/cargo_workspace_inheritance,_dotted_key
    ScipProjectVersion = "", want "3.3.3"
```

in this PR), `CONTAINS` counted 2, `DEFINES` counted 0.

## Finding responses — three open findings, two valid, one refuted

Head is now `30d490af`.

---

### 1. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:183` — Windows junctions are `ModeIrregular`, not `ModeSymlink` — **VALID**

The guard tested `info.Mode()&fs.ModeSymlink != 0`. That is the right test on Unix and the wrong one on Windows: a symlink is reported as `ModeSymlink`, but a directory junction or mount point is reported as `ModeIrregular`. A junction planted at the `family` or `version` component therefore passed the check and was then descended into and followed — exactly the redirect this guard exists to refuse.

This repository already had the correct predicate, with five production call sites:

```
internal/sem/path_redirect_windows.go:12   return info.Mode()&(os.ModeSymlink|os.ModeIrregular) != 0
internal/sem/path_redirect_other.go:8      return info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0
```
callers: `provider.go:11777`, `provider.go:13200`, `provider.go:15057`, `sweep_open_other.go:68`, `metadata_tree_entry_windows.go:37` — all in `package sem`, so it is a drop-in here.

**Fix:** `openCacheComponent` now calls `cacheComponentRedirectError`, which tests `pathMayRedirect(info)`. The message keeps the substring `is a symlink` that `search_cache_test.go:161` matches on, and names the mode it found.

---

### 2. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:194` — `rand.Text()` terminates the process — **VALID** (and stronger than described)

Verified in the toolchain's own source. `crypto/rand.Text` calls `Read`, and `crypto/rand/rand.go`:

```go
// Read calls [io.ReadFull] on [Reader] and crashes the program irrecoverably if
// an error is returned. …
	if err != nil {
		fatal("crypto/rand: failed to read random data (see https://go.dev/issue/66821): " + err.Error())
		panic("unreachable") // To be sure.
	}
```

`fatal` is `runtime.fatal` via `go:linkname`, reaching `fatalthrow` — the runtime's unrecoverable throw. So it is **not** a panic a caller can `recover`; it is a hard process kill. Tearing down a whole index run because a temporary cache file could not be named is the wrong failure mode for a best-effort write whose errors every caller already discards.

For contrast, `os.CreateTemp` never has this exposure: `$GOROOT/src/os/tempfile.go` names its files from `runtime.rand()`, an infallible non-cryptographic source. This code wants the CSPRNG for the O_EXCL race guard, so the answer is not to drop to a weaker source but to read it through an interface that reports.

**Fix:** `cacheTempNameSuffix(source io.Reader)` reads 16 bytes with `io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, …)` and hex-encodes them — same CSPRNG, error returned instead of a process kill.

---

### 3. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:186` — TOCTOU between `Lstat` and `OpenRoot` — **REFUTED**

The race window is real; the consequence it implies is not. `os.Root` enforces confinement inside the syscall, independently of any `Lstat` the caller did first, so winning the race cannot make the write escape the cache root.

Standalone probe against the same toolchain (`go1.26.0 darwin/arm64`), exercising every operation this code performs through the returned handle:

```
A OpenRoot(link -> ../outside RELATIVE): ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
B OpenRoot(link -> ABS outside path):    ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
C OpenRoot(link -> sibling INSIDE root): OK (no error)
C sub.Open(in.txt):                      SUCCESS, read "INSIDE-BYTES"
D OpenFile(link/x -> ../outside REL):    ERROR: openat link/x: path escapes from parent
E OpenFile(link/y -> ABS outside path):  ERROR: openat link/y: path escapes from parent
F Rename(src.txt -> link/z.txt):         ERROR: renameat src.txt link/z.txt: path escapes from parent
```

`go doc os.Root`:

> Methods on Root will follow symbolic links, but symbolic links may not reference a location outside the root. Symbolic links must not be absolute.

So the worst a won race can do is case C: redirect the write to **another location inside the same cache root**, which `os.Root` permits by design. That is not a privilege gain — whoever can plant the symlink at that component already has write access to the cache directory and can simply write the target path directly. The `Lstat` is a nicer error ahead of an enforcement that happens anyway, not the boundary itself.

No change made. Closing the window would mean re-deriving through a handle `os.Root` already re-derives, for an outcome `os.Root` already guarantees.

(The one documented exception is `GOOS=js`, where `os.Root` states it *is* vulnerable to symlink TOCTOU and cannot ensure confinement. This tool is not built for js/wasm.)

---

### Tests

In `internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`:

- `TestCacheComponentRedirectErrorHonoursEveryRedirectingMode` — table over `ModeDir`, `ModeSymlink`, `ModeIrregular|ModeDir`, presented through a stub `os.FileInfo`. The `ModeIrregular` row expects a refusal only where `runtime.GOOS == "windows"`, and expects **no** refusal elsewhere, so it also pins that ordinary irregular entries are not broken on platforms with no reparse points. A junction cannot be created in-process (privileges + `mklink`), and the guard either honours the bit or does not.
- `TestCacheTempNameSuffixReportsRandomnessFailure` — an erroring source and a short source must both be reported.
- `TestCacheTempNameSuffixIsUnpredictable` — 64 distinct 32-character lowercase-hex draws.
- `TestCreateRootTempNamesTheFileFromTheReportedRandomSource` — the call-site guard; the hex shape is what distinguishes it from `rand.Text`.

### Mutation verification

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `cacheTempNameSuffix` swallows the read error (`_ = err`) | **caught** — `cacheTempNameSuffix error = <nil>, want it to report randomness source unavailable` |
| `createRootTemp` reverted to `rand.Text()` | **caught** — `temporary cache file named ".REDACTED.json.gz", want .snapshot-<32 hexadecimal>.json.gz` |
| guard forced to accept everything (`if true \|\| !pathMayRedirect(info)`) | **caught** — symlink row fails |
| non-Windows `pathMayRedirect` widened to include `ModeIrregular` | **caught** — `mode d?--------- was refused on darwin` |
| guard reverted to `ModeSymlink`-only | **not caught on darwin, as expected** — the two predicates are identical on this platform by construction. That row discriminates only where the modes differ, i.e. on the `windows-latest` leg of `test.yml`. Stated rather than papered over. |

Each mutation was `grep`-confirmed applied before running, and the restore `grep`-confirmed after. `go test ./internal/sem -run 'Cache|Snapshot|Symlink|Confin'` passes; `go vet` and `gofmt -l` clean.

  - GitHub says mergeable/unstable, but it is 121 commits behind.

  - 4 files, `+312/-23`, 2 commits.
  - Conflicts with current `main`; 121 commits behind.
  - Trail #129: 2 open medium findings, 1 current/1 stale; no approvals.
  - Verified blocker: conversion operators are truncated at the first `(`. Valid `operator decltype(value)() const` becomes `operator decltype`, causing incorrect/colliding symbol IDs. The earlier ordinary `operator_name` issue appears fixed but remains stale/open in the trail.
  - **Verdict:** second after a focused operator-cast fix and conflict resolution.

- **#174 — extract C/C++ data members**
  - 4 files, `+474/-7`, 3 commits.
  - Conflicts with current `main`; 121 commits behind.
  - Trail #133: 4 open findings, 2 current/2 stale, plus 3 resolved; no approvals.
  - Verified blockers:
    - Broad parenthesized-declarator handling classifies valid `virtual int (Run)() = 0;` as a field, removing the callable.
    - Field signature/body hash keeps only the base type, so `char *data` becomes effectively `data char`; pointer/reference/array/function-pointer changes can become invisible to entity diff/impact.
  - **Verdict:** not ready. Fix both regressions and rebase. It is also the prerequisite for #177.

    - Out-of-line matching uses raw `strings.Contains`, allowing `A::foo` to match `BA::foo` and missing templated `A<T>::foo`.
    - The stale `#if/#ifdef`-wrapped declaration omission still appears unaddressed.
  - **Verdict:** cannot precede #174 and still needs correctness fixes afterward.

  - 3 files, `+717/-46`, 5 commits; broad resolver behavior change.

  - Trail #142: 5 open medium findings, 2 current/3 stale; no approvals.
  - Verified design blockers:
    - The C/C++/Objective-C/Swift relation is symmetric although interoperability is directional; it still invents impossible C→C++/Swift-style bindings.
    - A type-sharing predicate is reused for calls, dropping legitimate Zsh calls into sourced Bash `.sh` libraries.
    - The current diff still filters `TESTS` through the same predicate, so cross-language test harness relations can disappear; that stale finding remains materially present.
  - **Verdict:** last. This needs relation-specific, directional compatibility rules rather than a small patch.

None of #150, #146, #143, #142, or #141 is merge-ready against current `main` (`ee6468a6`).

Recommended remediation order:

1. #146 — smallest and least conflicting, but still draft with two contract defects.
2. #143 — mergeable and standard CI green, but its current finding weakens the core security guarantee.
3. #150 — narrow change, but conflicting and has two substantive regressions.
4. #141 — one current defect, but very large and conflicting.
5. #142 — conflicting, standard CI failing, and two budget/cancellation gaps.

Key blockers:

- #150: 121 behind and conflicting; two current Medium trail findings. It can OOM while buffering the index and omits an unstaged regular file replacing a symlink. Must integrate merged #166 and bump current cache versions from v10/v14, not restore old v9/v13.
- #146: draft, 86 behind, Entire gate red. Besides the current `/v1` → `/v1.0` contract break, its proposed failure-to-SCIP-Document join cannot handle `E_FILE_READ` or `E_UNSUPPORTED_LANGUAGE`, which emit no file record or Document. It should precede #152 if ADR numbering remains 0005/0006.
- #143: 81 behind, Entire gate red. RTL rows are detected but only prefixed with a space; bidi rendering moves that space to the opposite edge, leaving a forged `VERIFY:` at column zero. The implementation relies on a disclosure rather than actually quarantining that row.
- #141: 86 behind and conflicting. Its disclosure is written in addition to results already fitted to the full byte budget, violating `--max-context-bytes`.
- #142: 86 behind and conflicting. macOS CI fails because a canceled `git ls-tree` path returns `signal: killed` instead of `context.DeadlineExceeded`; Windows was canceled. The SCIP project-version lookup also bypasses the new budget guard.

All five Entire trails have zero approvals and at least one current Medium finding. I made no worktree changes and did not claim any tests beyond GitHub CI evidence.

Payload:
Recommendation to parent: merge none of this batch as-is. #160 is the closest and should be next after updating onto `main`, rerunning CI, and closing its trail.

Common state:

- All five branches are 121 commits behind `main` (`ee6468a6`).
- GitHub-required checks are green; the non-required Entire Gates check is red on every PR.
- Every trail remains `phase=building`, has zero approvals, and every PR commit lacks an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
- I ran no branch tests; test claims below are GitHub CI evidence only.

Ranking:

1. **#160 — cache write confinement**: +620/−113, 6 files. Mergeable; #154 dependency is merged with its compatibility fix. Latest CI was green across platforms on Aug 30. Trail has three stale-open findings and no current-freshness findings; two were fixed and one TOCTOU concern was rebutted credibly. Remaining concern: it deliberately breaks currently working in-root symlinked family layouts such as `cache/search -> cache/bigstore`, while its rationale says no working layout is lost. That compatibility decision should be acknowledged/documented. Closest to ready after refresh and trail approval.

2. **#153 — SCIP follow-ups**: +290/−2, 4 files. Mergeable; #97 already merged. CI green on Sep 2 except Entire Gates. Not ready: the latest Entire review found a real medium issue—standard virtual Cargo workspaces put `[workspace.package].version` in the root but `version.workspace=true` only in member manifests; because export reads only the root and this patch requires root `[package]` inheritance, identities still fall back to `0`. A low malformed-inline-table finding also remains. Cursor’s trailing-comment bug was fixed, but review was not rerun and its finding remains open.

3. **#161 — Julia module calls**: +166/−4, 2 files. Mergeable; #171 is merged and its language-matrix integration was prepared. CI green on Aug 30 except Entire Gates. Two current medium trail blockers are valid: module blocks gain bogus `Module -> child function` CALLS from declaration scanning, and a globally unique non-Julia method can become the target of an unresolved Julia call. Needs code fixes and refreshed CI.

4. **#152 — RFD 0006**: +214 docs-only, 2 files. Mergeable but still draft. No trail findings, but no approval or completed trail. It intentionally depends on draft #146 claiming ADR/RFD 0005; current `main` still contains only 0001–0004. Wait for #146 and an explicit RFD decision.

5. **#163 — F# pipelines**: +403/−10, 3 files. Now `CONFLICTING` because complementary #178 merged. CI was green on Aug 30 only. Trail has five open findings: two current medium blockers—ambiguous root-versus-nested module suffix matching and spurious module-level CALLS—and three stale-open findings. It needs rebase/conflict resolution plus substantive fixes before reconsideration.

Validation is complete: #160 merges cleanly onto current `main`, and the merged `internal/sem` suite passed in 270.5s. I’m doing one final freshness check now; barring a just-pushed change, the decision is “merge none today, prepare #160 next.”

  "number": 119,

  "base": "main",
  "title": "fix(sem): confine cache artifact writes to the cache directory",
  "body": "Now I have the full context. Let me create the summary:\nProblem:\nCache artifact writes were not confined to the cache directory. When a symlink was planted at a predictable cache component (family, version, or artifact name), writes would follow it outside the cache boundary — especially problematic when --cache-dir or ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR resolved inside a repository checkout, where the repository itself could plant such links. Reads already protected against this via os.OpenRoot, but the asymmetry meant a symlinked escape path would receive writes but no reads, silently creating permanent cache misses.\nSolution:\nCache writes now refuse any symlinked component beneath the cache root directory. The cacheEntry.write() method uses os.OpenRoot with component-by-component descent through openCacheDirectory(), checking each path component with Lstat and rejecting symlinks before descending. Temporary files are created and renamed within the opened handle, so an artifact symlink cannot redirect the bytes. The cache root itself may still be a symlink (supporting deployments that link the entire cache elsewhere), but all descendants named by Entire Graph are protected. Writes to a symlink-escaped path now fail with an explicit error (\"cache directory component %q is a symlink\"), and best-effort callers discard the error while explicit persist paths report it. The refusal is case-insensitive, and the atomicity guarantees of os.Rename apply even when the artifact name itself is a symlink, replacing the link rather than following it. Documentation in docs/trust-and-security.md updated to clarify the boundary.",

  "body": "Now I have the full context. Let me create the summary:\nProblem:\nCache artifact writes were not confined to the cache directory. When a symlink was planted at a predictable cache component (family, version, or artifact name), writes would follow it outside the cache boundary — especially problematic when --cache-dir or ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR resolved inside a repository checkout, where the repository itself could plant such links. Reads already protected against this via os.OpenRoot, but the asymmetry meant a symlinked escape path would receive writes but no reads, silently creating permanent cache misses.\nSolution:\nCache writes now refuse any symlinked component beneath the cache root directory. The cacheEntry.write() method uses os.OpenRoot with component-by-component descent through openCacheDirectory(), checking each path component with Lstat and rejecting symlinks before descending. Temporary files are created and renamed within the opened handle, so an artifact symlink cannot redirect the bytes. The cache root itself may still be a symlink (supporting deployments that link the entire cache elsewhere), but all descendants named by Entire Graph are protected. Writes to a symlink-escaped path now fail with an explicit error (\"cache directory component %q is a symlink\"), and best-effort callers discard the error while explicit persist paths report it. The refusal is case-insensitive, and the atomicity guarantees of os.Rename apply even when the artifact name itself is a symlink, replacing the link rather than following it. Documentation in docs/trust-and-security.md updated to clarify the boundary.",

item.stdout:
30d490af2a65b805d8483d1949b1880ffe593a09
fix(sem): honour every redirecting mode and report randomness failures
Two hardening follow-ups on the cache write path.

The component guard tested ModeSymlink alone. That is the right test on
Unix and the wrong one on Windows, which reports a symlink as ModeSymlink
but a directory junction or mount point as ModeIrregular: a junction planted
at the family or version component passed the check and was then descended
into and followed. The guard now uses pathMayRedirect, the predicate the
provider already applies at its other redirect boundaries, so the platform's
own notion of "this entry redirects" decides.

createRootTemp named its file with crypto/rand.Text, which reports a
randomness failure through runtime.fatal — an unrecoverable process kill,
not a panic a caller can recover. A best-effort cache write whose errors
every caller already discards would have torn down the whole index run.
Reading rand.Reader directly keeps the same CSPRNG and returns the failure
instead.

The redirecting-mode test presents the mode through a stub FileInfo, because
a Windows junction needs privileges and an mklink subprocess to create, and
the guard either honours the bit or does not. The temp-name test pins the
32-hexadecimal shape, which is what ties the call site to the reporting draw
rather than to rand.Text's 26 uppercase base32 characters.

---
90fc71c98db33b4a360055c37bd5dfba11cfd4b0
test(sem): assert the cache artifact mode only where mode bits exist
Windows has no Unix permission bits: Go synthesizes FileMode there from the
read-only attribute alone, so the artifact created 0600 reads back 0666 and the
assertion tested the platform rather than the write. Guard it on GOOS and keep
it exact everywhere it means something -- a write that produced 0644 still fails
the check on Unix.

---
5f99842e63ec8d3aca04221218994e56f11fb1c4
fix(sem): confine cache artifact writes to the cache directory
The search-snapshot and provider-records caches installed their artifact with
os.MkdirAll + os.CreateTemp + os.Rename on the joined path, so a symlinked
directory component decided where the artifact actually landed. --cache-dir and
ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR accept a path inside the scanned checkout, and there the
component is a committed symlink: a repository could redirect the write out of
the cache directory, or into its own .git.

Reads already go through os.OpenRoot(cacheDir), which refuses those components,
so such an entry was written on every run and read on none -- a silent permanent
cache miss as well as a write the repository steered.

cacheEntry.write now creates each component below the root and Lstat-checks it
before descending into it through its own handle, refusing a symlink. os.Root
alone is not enough: it stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays
inside it, and with the cache directory at a checkout root, .git is inside it.
The temporary file is a crypto/rand name opened O_CREATE|O_EXCL inside that
checked handle, and the install is a Rename within it.

A symlinked cache directory -- the cache on another volume, in a shared
location, outside a container's writable layer -- is caller-named and still
resolved as given, on both sides.

---

directory component decided where the artifact actually landed. --cache-dir and
ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR accept a path inside the scanned checkout, and there the
component is a committed symlink: a repository could redirect the write out of
the cache directory, or into its own .git.

Reads already go through os.OpenRoot(cacheDir), which refuses those components,
so such an entry was written on every run and read on none -- a silent permanent
cache miss as well as a write the repository steered.

cacheEntry.write now creates each component below the root and Lstat-checks it
before descending into it through its own handle, refusing a symlink. os.Root
alone is not enough: it stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays
inside it, and with the cache directory at a checkout root, .git is inside it.
The temporary file is a crypto/rand name opened O_CREATE|O_EXCL inside that
checked handle, and the install is a Rename within it.

A symlinked cache directory -- the cache on another volume, in a shared
location, outside a container's writable layer -- is caller-named and still
resolved as given, on both sides.

fix(sem): honour every redirecting mode and report randomness failures
Two hardening follow-ups on the cache write path.

The component guard tested ModeSymlink alone. That is the right test on
Unix and the wrong one on Windows, which reports a symlink as ModeSymlink
but a directory junction or mount point as ModeIrregular: a junction planted
at the family or version component passed the check and was then descended
into and followed. The guard now uses pathMayRedirect, the predicate the
provider already applies at its other redirect boundaries, so the platform's
own notion of "this entry redirects" decides.

createRootTemp named its file with crypto/rand.Text, which reports a
randomness failure through runtime.fatal — an unrecoverable process kill,
not a panic a caller can recover. A best-effort cache write whose errors
every caller already discards would have torn down the whole index run.
Reading rand.Reader directly keeps the same CSPRNG and returns the failure
instead.

The redirecting-mode test presents the mode through a stub FileInfo, because
a Windows junction needs privileges and an mklink subprocess to create, and
the guard either honours the bit or does not. The temp-name test pins the
32-hexadecimal shape, which is what ties the call site to the reporting draw
rather than to rand.Text's 26 uppercase base32 characters.

test(sem): assert the cache artifact mode only where mode bits exist
Windows has no Unix permission bits: Go synthesizes FileMode there from the
read-only attribute alone, so the artifact created 0600 reads back 0666 and the
assertion tested the platform rather than the write. Guard it on GOOS and keep
it exact everywhere it means something -- a write that produced 0644 still fails
the check on Unix.

fix(sem): confine cache artifact writes to the cache directory
The search-snapshot and provider-records caches installed their artifact with
os.MkdirAll + os.CreateTemp + os.Rename on the joined path, so a symlinked
directory component decided where the artifact actually landed. --cache-dir and
ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR accept a path inside the scanned checkout, and there the
component is a committed symlink: a repository could redirect the write out of
the cache directory, or into its own .git.

Reads already go through os.OpenRoot(cacheDir), which refuses those components,
so such an entry was written on every run and read on none -- a silent permanent
cache miss as well as a write the repository steered.

cacheEntry.write now creates each component below the root and Lstat-checks it
before descending into it through its own handle, refusing a symlink. os.Root
alone is not enough: it stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays
inside it, and with the cache directory at a checkout root, .git is inside it.
The temporary file is a crypto/rand name opened O_CREATE|O_EXCL inside that
checked handle, and the install is a Rename within it.

A symlinked cache directory -- the cache on another volume, in a shared
location, outside a container's writable layer -- is caller-named and still
resolved as given, on both sides.

Recommendation: accept strict refusal of all descendant cache redirects, including in-root symlinks, but first fix the TOCTOU gap and correct the compatibility claims.

Key conclusions:

- `main` deliberately allows descendant symlinks for writes.
- Escaping links write successfully but cannot be read through `os.Root`, so the claimed larger-volume/shared-cache layouts are permanent misses.
- In-root links such as `cache/search -> cache/bigstore` genuinely work today. PR #160 therefore does break compatibility; “costs nothing that works today” is incorrect.
- The break is justified: with the cache rooted at a checkout, a committed version link can steer the digest-named artifact into `.git/refs/heads` or another repository-chosen directory. The realistic impact is metadata pollution, denial of service, and arbitrary cache-file placement—not a demonstrated chosen-file overwrite or RCE.
- Root-level symlinking preserves the useful relocation cases, leaving only a narrow in-root-alias use case.

Do not dismiss the TOCTOU finding. `Lstat` followed by `OpenRoot` does not enforce the promised no-redirect property. Use the already-proven pattern from `outputpath.go`: open the component first, compare `parent.Lstat(name)` with `held.Stat(".")` using `os.SameFile`, then operate only through the held handle.

The randomness and Windows findings are fixed by `30d490af` and can be resolved. The TOCTOU finding should be fixed, then resolved.

Before approval, require:

- Explicit operations documentation that only the cache root may be a symlink; family/version descendants may not redirect, even in-root.
- Migration guidance: point `--cache-dir` or `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` at the backing directory, or symlink the root.
- Removal of the false “nothing working is lost” and “internal entries are never read” claims.
- A test explicitly refusing a benign in-root alias such as `search -> bigstore`.

content.text:
PR #160 now has two findings resolved and one open:

- Resolved: randomness failure handling.
- Resolved: Windows junction/reparse-point handling.
- Open: `Lstat`→`OpenRoot` TOCTOU race; it still permits an in-root redirect swap.

A policy decision is required:

entire session adopt — Adopt an active session from another worktree
Adopt an active session from another worktree into the current repository.

This is useful when an agent starts in one repository or worktree, then moves
and makes changes in another. Adoption moves the live session state into the
current repo and seeds it with the current repo's uncommitted file changes so
the next commit can be linked normally.

When the source and target share a Git session store, adoption moves the same
session state file to the current worktree and requires --force or --yes.

- Local release builds require `tar` for non-Windows archives, `zip` or `7z`

## Cache

Queries build a snapshot of the repository graph and cache it as compressed
derivative state. Nothing in the cache modifies repository files, and deleting
the cache directory costs a rebuild, nothing else.

### Location

The cache root is resolved in order: `--cache-dir`, then
`ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR`, then the per-user cache directory (`entire-graph`
under the OS user cache path). The per-user fallback applies to `search`,
`neighbors`, `impact`, `index`, `snapshot`, `symbols`, and `edges`. `def` and
`explain` stop at `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR`; with neither the flag nor the
variable set they rebuild on every run. One directory is shared by every
repository and worktree on the machine; keys, not directories, separate
entries.

### Two cache families

- The **search snapshot cache** backs `search`, `neighbors`, `impact`, and
  `index`. It caches committed-tree (`--head`) queries; working-tree queries
  always bypass it.
- The **provider records cache** backs the bulk streams (`snapshot`,
  `symbols`, `edges`). It is committed-tree only; `--worktree` streams always
  bypass it.

### What a cache entry is keyed on

A search-snapshot entry is a function of: the cache format version, the
checkout path, the repository identity (derived from the Git remote), the
provider version, the committed `HEAD` tree hash, the profile, the parse-size
and file-count limits, any file-subset selection, the paths **and contents** of
`--ignore-file`/`--include-file` inputs in caller order, and the contents of
`.graphignore`. Change any of these and the next query builds a new entry;
matching all of them is what "cache hit" means. A legacy worktree discriminator
remains in the envelope only to reject retired entries; it is not a current key
term because working-tree snapshots cannot receive persistent keys.
[ADR 0002](adr/0002-committed-tree-cache-key.md) records why the key is total
over graph-shaping inputs.

A provider-record entry binds the same graph-shaping inputs plus the exact
commit and output mode. Exact commit identity is required because the cached
opaque NDJSON header records it; unlike a structured search snapshot, that
stream cannot be safely restamped on a same-tree cache hit.

### Working-tree queries

Interactive queries default to the working tree and always build a fresh

One actionable finding:

- [P2] Documentation overstates POSIX mount-point refusal. `docs/operations.md:64-66` and `docs/trust-and-security.md:182-185` say all mount points are refused. On non-Windows, `pathMayRedirect` only checks `ModeSymlink`; for a POSIX mount point, `parent.Lstat(name)` and `held.Stat(".")` both describe the mounted root, so `os.SameFile` succeeds and the component is accepted. Either qualify this as “Windows junctions and mount-point reparse entries” or add explicit POSIX mount detection.

Finding `01M1398TQ21XQG69F04WT8FVNR` is otherwise fully fixed:

- The component is opened before validation.
- A fresh `Lstat` is compared against `held.Stat(".")` with `os.SameFile`.
- Subsequent operations use the held `os.Root`, so later name swaps cannot redirect them to a different object.
- `next` is closed on every validation failure and transferred to the caller only on success; no handle leak found.
- Windows symlink/junction checks still run before identity acceptance.
- Raw filesystem errors remain propagated, while redirect cases retain the actionable cache-component diagnostic.

No other actionable correctness, TOCTOU, handle-lifecycle, cross-platform identity, or error-contract issue found.
